findings.where: Phone first screen: the order of the heading, the yellow 'Write to me directly' strip and the 'I advise multilateral development banks…' paragraph
findings.fault: On a phone, the page asks for an email before it says what Mark does. The address strip comes straight after the heading, and the only sentence naming his work and his clients sits below it, past the first phone screen. Someone who opens the link on a phone sees a name, a photo and an opinion, then a request to write. Only after that do they learn the service and who it is for.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank staffer who opens the site from LinkedIn on a phone. In five seconds they cannot tell whether he advises their kind of organisation. Being asked to write before the offer is clear reads as a sales move, and that is the 'salesy' failure the brief warns against.

findings.where: First screen, the hero heading 'In my view, we are at a turning point in the story of public-private partnerships.'
findings.fault: The heading promises an argument that the page never delivers. Nothing on the first screen says what the turning point is, and the heading doesn't link to the piece it comes from (Blog No. 2, 2020). The line reads as a teaser with no follow-through. Without the paragraph below it, it says what is happening in PPP, not what Mark offers.
findings.who_objects: A procurement reader judging his judgement. They are told he has a view and given no way to read it. The founder wants Mark heard, and here his voice is reduced to a slogan-length claim with nothing behind it on the page.

findings.where: First screen: the name block, the credential line and the supporting paragraph
findings.fault: The page never says where Mark is based or in which regions he has worked. First-visit trust item 6 (location) always applies, and an international advisor should show the regions of his work. The heading and the paragraph speak only of PPP in general.
findings.who_objects: Staff at a multilateral development bank who pick consultants by region and project kind under terms of reference. They cannot tell whether he has worked in their region, which the rules name as the first thing an advisor's visitor must be sure of.

findings.where: Article specimen, the Download row 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the ‘Abundance’ Challenge — Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF'
findings.fault: The newest talk is listed with its date but not its venue or who invited him. That fact would turn the lecture into proof of standing. 'Feel the CV' asks for the newest talk to be shown with its venue.
findings.who_objects: A bank or agency reader. For them, 'who asked him to speak' is the evidence, and a bare 'Lecture' could have been given anywhere.

findings.where: Navigation (Profile · Articles · Blog) and the end of the article specimen
findings.fault: The navigation has no 'Contact' label. The address appears only in the home hero, and the article specimen ends on a download with no address or identity line. A reader who lands on an article from a social post has no visible way to reach Mark (first-visit trust items 7 and 12, and the Clashes table's Contact label).
findings.who_objects: A development-agency reader who arrives on an article from LinkedIn, is persuaded by it and wants to write. They have to guess that the address is on the home page.

findings.where: First screen as a whole: the only proof is the 'Formerly Lead Lawyer, PPP Group, World Bank' line
findings.fault: The first screen has no evidence of work beyond one former job title. There are no named bodies that asked for his work, no recent mandate and no link to work that named bodies host. Third-party proof is absent.
findings.who_objects: A procurement-minded reader who wants checkable specifics before writing. One past title says where he worked, not what he has done since or for whom.
